01 What Danger Close Does ↑ Contents

In plain English — start here

Picture your retirement as one long road trip where nobody can tell you the weather ahead of time. This app drives that whole trip thousands of times. Some runs get sunshine (strong markets); some hit storms (a crash, years of high inflation, a long illness). Each run, it checks whether you still have money when the trip ends.

So when you see "success rate 90%," it means: across 10,000 imagined futures, your savings lasted in about 9,000 of them. Think of it as a weather forecast for your money — useful odds, never a promise.

At its core, the app does six things, all locally in your browser:

  1. Holds your portfolio and household context — positions, balances, Roth/Traditional split, asset classes, names, DOBs, Social Security, pension, housing, goals — which you type into the My Data tab or restore from a saved backup file.
  2. Runs Monte Carlo simulations at the asset-class level using six probability-weighted economic regimes (base, optimistic, pessimistic, recession, stagflation, crisis) at 5,000–10,000 iterations.
  3. Models the retirement transition quarter-by-quarter through year 30 — Social Security claiming, pension start, Roth conversions, home sale and cash purchase, Medicare and the ACA bridge, and long-term care.
  4. Builds a withdrawal schedule — a year-by-year plan of which account funds each year's spending, with account-priority sequencing.
  5. Stress-tests the plan against named adverse scenarios and reverse-solves for the break-points.
  6. Provides an Ask AI tab that sends a structured summary to an AI assistant for natural-language follow-up.
This tool assumes you already have a retirement plan and want to pressure-test it. It is not a "what is a 401(k)" tool. Nothing is uploaded to any server except the calls you explicitly send from the Ask AI tab.
Why "Danger Close"? In artillery, danger close is the call that supporting fire is landing near your own position — the moment that demands maximum precision because the stakes are highest. That's the metaphor, and the whole reason this tool exists: the years surrounding retirement are when a financial mistake lands closest to home, and the math deserves artillery-grade care. To be clear about the styling: the author is a civilian, has never served in the military, and claims no service — the name and the console aesthetic are a design theme borrowed with respect for what the term means.

What's new in v5.6 (this build)

For anyone upgrading from an earlier copy, the headline changes: a 🧭 Guided Setup wizard (landing screen + My Data) that builds a working plan from six questions; Simple Mode (six core tabs, one-click switch, remembered); a Dashboard tab answering the three questions retirees actually ask, now the default landing view; a 51-jurisdiction state-tax model; Roth upgrades — a 25-cell solve-for optimizer and a conversion-tax funding model (cash vs appreciated-brokerage sale vs withholding from the conversion); Social Security upgrades — breakeven cards for both spouses (with the first-death horizon twist for the lower earner) and an 81-cell joint claiming-age grid; Monte Carlo engine toggles for stochastic longevity and a realistic LTC duration distribution (§06 explains both); a threaded, memory-keeping Ask AI conversation with an Offline Mode hard switch and a local-model option; a data-vintage staleness system (§13); a first-open rendering bug fixed; the Compare tab and the FICO field retired; and a 48-check validation suite asserting every statutory constant against IRS/CMS/SSA sources.

02 How Data Flows Through It ↑ Contents

Everything starts from one in-memory model (PORTFOLIO + PLAN_TIMELINE), and every tab derives its numbers from that single source. You fill that model one of three ways: type your data into the My Data tab, restore a backup you exported earlier (a JSON file), or load the example household to explore. Whatever you enter is saved privately between visits so the app reopens to your plan, and you can export it to a JSON file to keep or move between devices. Nothing is ever shared, and the only transmission of plan data is the summary the Ask AI tab sends when you explicitly ask a question.

In plain English

There's no account and nothing to sign up for. The app keeps one private copy of your plan just for you. You either type it in or hand it a backup file you saved before — and everything else you see, every tab, chart, and score, is calculated from that one copy on the spot. Nobody else ever sees it; the only thing that transmits anything is the Ask AI tab, when you press ask.

Because every tab derives from one model, the app is fully portable: load a different household and every visible number re-derives. Income figures route through single accessors, so there are no scattered hard-coded values.

04 The Data-Integrity Warning Banner ↑ Contents

To keep the app from quietly showing you someone else's numbers, it tracks where each income figure (Social Security, pension) came from. A banner appears at the top of every tab in two flavors — and understanding when each one can fire tells you how the protection actually works:

⚠ WARNING — USING EXAMPLE NUMBERS, NOT YOUR DATA (red)

Fires when your plan arrived without income figures of its own — typically an older backup, or a plan saved before the My Data income section existed — and the app had to substitute the demo household's numbers to keep the engines running. It names exactly which fields were substituted (e.g. "Spouse B Social Security, Pension") and includes a small diagnostics line showing what it looked for and what it found. Until you enter the real amounts in My Data → Income and press Save & Apply, every projection that uses income — taxes, IRMAA, survivor, withdrawals — is unreliable.

ⓘ EXAMPLE DATA MODE (amber)

The gentle version. Fires when you deliberately chose "Use Example Data." All figures are illustrative placeholders; no alarm needed.

What about income you simply haven't entered yet? That's the third case, and it works differently by design: an income field left blank in My Data is saved as an honest $0 — the app never swaps a demo number in behind your form entries. A zero is your number, just probably not your final number, so instead of a banner you'll see it plainly as $0 on the Income tab and in the header's income floor. The red banner is reserved for the genuinely dangerous case: figures that look real but belong to the demo household.

When your own numbers are all in place, no banner appears — the check costs nothing day-to-day but flags instantly if a demo figure ever stands in for yours.

06 Top-Level Controls & Modeling Approach ↑ Contents

Controls

  • Retirement Date Selector — switches the modeled retirement quarter; recomputes the whole plan.
  • Scenario Prior Selector — BASE / BEAR-LEANING / BULL-LEANING. Re-weights the six economic regimes feeding the Monte Carlo.
  • Roth Conversion Amount (Roth tab) — $0–$120,000 (step $5,000), default $70,000/yr. The single biggest lever: it drives four tabs at once — Roth ladder, Withdrawal schedule, Taxes, and IRMAA — all from one shared value.
  • SS Claim-Age slider (SS tab) — 62–70, drives the claiming optimizer. The spouse names shown are read from your data (My Data tab), not hard-coded.
  • Guardrails Toggle (Trajectory tab) — show/hide the Guyton-Klinger spending bands.

Modeling Approach — read this

Danger Close uses a regime-switching mixture model — with two optional engine toggles on the Monte Carlo tab: stochastic longevity (Gompertz-sampled death ages anchored to your entered life expectancy as the median) and an LTC distribution (a drawn care-duration tail replacing the single shock) — not the classical mean-plus-standard-deviation Monte Carlo most tools use. Each year the simulator picks one of six regimes (under BASE: base 45%, optimistic 20%, pessimistic 15%, recession 10%, stagflation 7%, crisis 3%) and holds it for all four quarters — the regime means are annual outcomes — then applies that regime's return plus a small quarterly noise term. Variance comes mostly from regime-switching, so the AAGR-vs-CAGR "variance drag" double-counting bug that affects some tools does not apply here.

In plain English

Most calculators picture the market as one bumpy "average" year repeated over and over. Danger Close instead rolls a die each year to decide what kind of year it is — normal, boom, slump, recession, 1970s-style high-inflation, or 2008-style crisis — and uses that year's typical result. Real economies move in streaks (good years cluster together, so do bad ones), and picking a year-type each turn captures that far better than one fixed average.

But the BASE prior is deliberately conservative versus historical US equity performance. Probability-weighted across regimes:

Even the BULL-LEANING prior sits well below realized history. This is a modeling choice, not a bug — it follows the conservative-academic tradition (Pfau and others advocate 2–4% forward real returns for planning). In practice, your success rates here will read lower than Boldin/ProjectionLab/Pralana at their defaults, sometimes by 10–20 points. Cross-check critical results against one commercial tool; the gap is the prior's conservatism, not an error. For history-like output, use BULL-LEANING.

Inflation assumptions — one map, three different numbers on purpose

Three inflation figures appear in the app, and the differences are deliberate, each erring conservative in its own direction: (1) Household inflation ~2.7% expected — the simulators (Monte Carlo, Trajectory, Stress) don't use a single rate at all; each simulated quarter draws the regime's rate (2.0% in booms, 2.8% base, 3.5% pessimistic, 6.5% in stagflation — probability-weighted ≈2.7% under the BASE prior, between the last 30 years' ~2.5% and the full-century ~3.0%). Spending and Social Security's COLA ride these draws; the pension deliberately doesn't (no COLA). (2) Tax-threshold indexation 2.0% — brackets, deductions, and IRMAA tiers grow at 2%/yr in the deterministic tax engines. Law indexes these by chained CPI, which historically runs ~0.3 points below regular CPI — and for thresholds, assuming slower growth is the conservative choice: income outgrowing brackets produces bracket creep, so the model overstates your future taxes rather than flattering them. Raising this number would make Roth math look better, not safer. (3) LTC costs: inflation +1.5% — long-term-care costs escalate above whatever inflation each path draws, reflecting decades of care-cost growth outrunning CPI. Same philosophy every time: where an assumption must be picked, pick the direction that makes the plan look slightly worse than reality.

Why stochastic longevity matters — the STOCHASTIC LONGEVITY toggle

By default, the simulator assumes both of you live to exactly the life expectancies you entered — clean, transparent, and quietly unrealistic, because nobody dies on schedule. The STOCHASTIC LONGEVITY toggle on the Monte Carlo tab replaces that with something closer to life: each of the 10,000 runs samples a different death age for each spouse from a Gompertz mortality curve anchored so the life expectancy you entered is the median — a 50/50 over-under, not a guarantee. (Anchored at 88, for example, the sampled tenth percentile lands near 74 and the ninetieth near 98.) Your number keeps its meaning; the tails around it become real.

That matters because the two tails stress completely different parts of the plan:

  • Long-life runs — the portfolio stress test. Live well past the median — late 90s, even past 100 — and the danger is simply outliving the money: more spending years than planned, sequence-of-returns risk compounding over decades, inflation quietly halving purchasing power roughly every 24 years at 3%, and long-term-care odds rising exactly when the balance is smallest.
  • Short-life runs — the survivor stress test. One spouse dying early triggers the widowhood penalty: the household keeps only the larger Social Security check, most fixed expenses (housing, property taxes, insurance, utilities) barely shrink, the survivor is pushed into Single filing's narrower brackets and smaller standard deduction, and healthcare costs often rise. The Survivor tab dissects this case; the toggle folds thousands of variations of it into the headline success rate.
In plain English

Instead of asking "what happens if we live exactly to our life expectancies?", the toggle asks the better question: "what fraction of thousands of realistic lifetimes — some short, some very long — does this plan survive?" Expect the success number to move when you flip it; that movement is the information. One honest limit: the two spouses' lifespans are sampled independently — the real-world correlation of couples' health is not modeled.

The real shape of long-term-care risk — the LTC DISTRIBUTION toggle

Long-term-care duration is one of the most right-skewed risks in retirement — the average hides everything that matters. The research picture: roughly a third of today's 65-year-olds will never need long-term-care support at all; the median formal (nursing-home) stay is startlingly brief — often days or weeks of post-acute rehab after a surgery or illness; yet about 20% will need care for more than five years, and roughly 5% will spend over four years in a nursing home. Duration also splits sharply by sex — women average about 3.7 years of care need versus 2.2 for men, largely because women live longer (and spend about 6.1 adult years giving care besides). It is why the long-term-care insurance industry standardized on a 3-year benefit period: it covers the great majority of claims at a payable premium — while dementia care, the classic budget-breaker, routinely outruns it.

The default engine models care as one $150K–$300K event per spouse — the median-ish experience. The LTC DISTRIBUTION toggle swaps in the real shape: each run draws a paid-care duration per spouse (usually zero, occasionally many years, at ~$120K/yr in today's dollars escalating 1.5%/yr above inflation), anchored to the final years before that run's own death. The expected cost is similar to the single shock; the ruin tail is far fatter — because multi-year care lands at the worst possible moment: portfolio at its smallest, one Social Security check already gone.

In plain English — and one number reconciled

Most people pay little for care; a few pay catastrophically. Averages mislead; the toggle models the lottery instead. One apparent conflict worth squaring: research says ~33% never need any care, while this model draws "no paid care" 45% of the time — different measures, not a contradiction, since a large share of real care is unpaid family care that never touches a portfolio. Both agree on the part that matters: the tail, not the average, is the risk. Pair the toggle with the Stress tab's LTC Marathon — and if you are evaluating LTC insurance, this is exactly the distribution a 3-year benefit period is priced against.

▍Foundation

Dashboard foundation

One screen, the three questions retirees actually ask.

Will my money last? (Monte Carlo success and median outcome) · How much can I spend? (modeled spending, the guaranteed-income floor, and the resulting portfolio draw rate) · Can I survive a crash? (success with poor returns forced into the first three retirement years, vs the no-crash base). Each card links to the tab with the full workings. It's the default landing view once a plan is loaded — and a good place to send a spouse who wants the answer without the other tabs.

My Data foundation

Where your plan lives — the forms every other tab reads from.

Household (names, birth dates, retirement year, life expectancies, state tax), holdings, Social Security & pension, contributions, and expenses — plus Save & Apply, Export / Import Backup, and Clear All Data. Section 08 walks through every field. If a projection ever looks wrong, this tab is where to look first.

Trajectory foundation

The headline balance-over-time chart from now through year 30.

Shows the projected portfolio path with optional Guyton-Klinger guardrail bands. The first read for "does the line trend up, drift, or deplete?"

Expenses foundation

Pre- vs post-retirement spending, item by item.

Each expense shows its category, amount, and active window (start → end · duration). A delta block shows what drops off at retirement (e.g. mortgage), what adds on (LTC, ACA, Medicare), and what continues unchanged (marked ↻), with no double-counting.

Tip: recurring "for-life" costs (housing, food, utilities, Medicare) should run all the way to the end of the plan. If any stop early, the Events tab raises an alarm — otherwise the simulator treats those later years as free and every success rate looks rosier than it should.

Income foundation

Guaranteed income stack: Social Security, pension, part-time work.

Shows when each stream starts and the combined floor. The key insight it surfaces appears below.

When guaranteed income covers most of spending, the portfolio draw is tiny — the difference between "income-replacement capital" and "legacy capital." This single fact drives most of the app's reassuring results.

SS (Social Security) foundation

Claiming-age optimizer for both spouses.

A trust-fund depletion scenario panel sits at the top: per the 2026 Trustees Report, the retirement fund alone depletes in late 2032 (then ~78% of scheduled benefits payable — the legal default), or 2034/~83% if Congress merges it with the disability fund. Depletion is not bankruptcy — checks continue at the covered percentage — and Congress has always acted before a cut landed, which is why this is a scenario toggle, not a prediction: flip it and every simulation, the Roth tax engine, the Dashboard, and the claiming grid recompute with post-depletion checks at your chosen percentage (benefit tables and breakeven cards keep showing scheduled amounts for clarity). Three one-click choices — NO CUT (scheduled benefits, what your statement shows), 2033 → 78% (the OASI retirement fund alone — the legal default absent new law), 2034 → 83% (OASI+DI combined, which requires an act of Congress) — plus custom year/percent fields. When active, a readout shows exactly what happens to each spouse's check and the household total in dollars, with a guide to where the cut ripples. Persisted across sessions. Below it: benefit-by-claiming-age tables (62–70), crossover ages, and the lifetime trade-off of claiming early vs delaying. Names and amounts read from your data. For couples, a dedicated Spouse B breakeven card runs the same claim-early-vs-FRA arithmetic on the second record and adds the couple's twist: the smaller check only pays until the first death (the survivor keeps the larger one), so the lower earner's honest breakeven horizon is the joint first death — usually years shorter than their own life expectancy — while a higher-earning Spouse B's delay protects the survivor and runs to the second death. And a spousal claiming-age grid sweeps all 81 combinations of both spouses' claiming ages and scores household lifetime benefits (today's dollars, survivor step-up included, deaths at your entered life expectancies), marking the model's best cell against your current plan — with its approximations listed right under the grid (no discounting; spousal top-up benefits not modeled).

Positions foundation

The raw holdings table behind everything.

Every position with its balance, account type, Roth/Traditional split, and asset class — the audit trail for the rest of the app.

▍Scoring

Grade scoring

A composite retirement-readiness letter grade.

A radar chart across weighted dimensions (portfolio size, income floor, sequence buffer, LTC/tail risk, tax efficiency, diversification, estate readiness), with the evidence and the drag behind each grade.

Ranking scoring

Where you sit versus US peers.

Approximate "Top N%" tiers built from public survey data. The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF, currently the 2022 survey) is the backbone, with EBRI, SSA, and AALTCI filling in the rest. Heuristic context, not precise statistics — the percentile cut-points and the "Nx the average" ratios all trace back to these benchmarks.

Why two savings benchmarks? The SCF surveys the whole population of Americans 55–64, so it includes the ~25% with essentially nothing saved — which drags the average and median down and flatters anyone who has saved consistently. So the tab pairs it with an Empower Personal Dashboard benchmark: balances for people who actively track their money on that platform — a self-selected crowd whose balances run far higher. Read the SCF as the easy mirror (you'll be several multiples of the average) and Empower as the honest one (the savers you actually resemble). Two limits to keep in mind: the figures are hand-entered approximations, not live microdata, and the SCF refreshes only every three years — the 2025 survey publishes ~fall 2026, when the Events tab flags these benchmarks as due for a refresh.

▍Strategy

Guardrails strategy

Guyton-Klinger dynamic spending rules.

Cut spending if the portfolio falls to the lower band (default 80% of plan); raise it if it reaches the upper band (120%). Shows when each band triggers across scenarios.

Withdrawal Strategy strategy

A year-by-year operational drawdown plan.

Three sections: the year-by-year schedule, the account-priority order (Taxable → Traditional → Roth, with an 8-step order-of-operations), and a 3-strategy comparison. Growth rates link to the active scenario prior; the Roth-conversion column reads the shared slider.

Roth strategy

The Roth conversion ladder from retirement until the year before RMDs begin (RMD age 73 or 75 by birth year — SECURE 2.0).

Projects conversions year by year, the resulting RMD reduction at RMD age (73 for 1951–59 births, 75 for 1960+), current Traditional/Roth balances (derived from your positions), and break-even. The conversion window and RMD start are below.

⚠ PAY CONVERSION TAX FROM OUTSIDE FUNDS — NOT FROM RETIREMENT ASSETS

When you convert, the IRS wants its tax. Where that tax money comes from changes the math of the whole conversion. Pay it from a taxable (brokerage/savings) account and the full conversion lands in the Roth. Pay it by withholding from the conversion itself and you shrink the very tax shelter you are building — and if you are under 59½, you get fined for it.

Example 1 — age 59½+, $100K conversion at a 24% marginal rate, 20 years at 4.5% growth

  • Tax paid from outside funds: $100,000 enters the Roth → grows to $241,171, all tax-free. The $24,000 tax came from your taxable account.
  • Tax withheld from the conversion: only $76,000 enters the Roth → $183,290. The $24,000 you kept in taxable grows to about $52,800 after capital-gains tax. Total ≈ $236,089 — about $5,100 less, and that understates it because taxable dividends are taxed every year along the way.

The clean way to see it: paying from outside funds is equivalent to moving an extra $24,000 of taxable money inside the Roth wrapper — something contribution limits would never otherwise let you do. Withholding throws that free shelter space away.

Example 2 — the same conversion under age 59½: now it costs real money

The $24,000 withheld never reaches the Roth, so the IRS treats it as an early distribution: a 10% penalty = $2,400 in cash, gone immediately. Add the lost growth on that penalty and the wrapper loss from Example 1, and the total cost is roughly $10,900 per $100K converted. On a multi-year ladder this compounds: withholding 24% on a $70K/yr conversion costs $1,680/yr in pure penalty alone. This is the case where never really means never.

Example 3 — what if you have no taxable account?

Some households (including the built-in example) hold nearly everything in retirement accounts. Honest answer: conversions can still be worth doing — the Conversion Strategy Comparator on the Roth tab models taxes paid from the taxable account first and Roth second, and conversions still beat doing nothing for the example household — the benefit is simply smaller than with outside funds. If you are under 59½, avoid withholding specifically: pay the tax from current cash flow via estimated payments so the full conversion reaches the Roth and no penalty applies. If you are 59½+ with no outside funds, size conversions so the reduced benefit still clears the bar (low brackets, widow-penalty avoidance, RMD reduction).

Rule of thumb: under 59½, never withhold from a conversion. At any age, prefer outside funds — every tax dollar paid from inside the shelter is shelter you permanently lose.

Taxes strategy

Lifetime tax estimate: federal income, capital gains, FICA, state.

Lifetime summary cards plus a clickable year-by-year table. Each year breaks gross taxable income into its sources (SS taxable portion, pension, earned income, RMD, Roth conversion, cap gains) via a stacked bar, then subtracts deductions to net taxable and shows the bracket-by-bracket fill. State tax uses a 51-jurisdiction module (2026 approximations): each state's effective rate, Social Security treatment (only 8 states partially tax SS in 2026), full retirement-income exemptions (IL/MS/PA/IA/MI + the 9 no-tax states), and major 65+ exclusions (e.g. Georgia's $65K/person). Pick your state in My Data — or leave it on manual and the legacy flat rate applies unchanged. It is an approximation layer: effective rates stand in for progressive brackets and several income-limited exclusions are treated as unconditional — verify your state. The Roth slider drives the conversion column live, and a QCD what-if slider models charitable IRA distributions (income exclusion, RMD offset, lower MAGI). The tab reads as four numbered steps with a 30-second explainer up top: ① the conversion slider (your what-if dial — the comparator reads it live and names its row after it), ② the tax-funding selector, ③ the six-strategy comparator, ④ the solve-for grid. A conversion-tax funding control models where the tax money actually comes from — the question most calculators skip. Three honest cases: a sale that creates no taxable profit (cash, money markets, or an account holding little growth), an appreciated brokerage sale (the engine grosses the sale up to cover the capital-gains tax the sale itself creates — long-term rates stacked on that year's income — and feeds the realized gains into MAGI so the IRMAA lookback two years later sees them), or withholding from the conversion itself for households with no outside money (no sale, no gains tax, permanently smaller Roth — sometimes still the winning move; "never pay conversion tax from the IRA" assumes outside cash you may not have). Approximations, stated plainly: one blended gain share for the whole account, all long-term, no per-lot selection, no loss harvesting, no wash-sale logic, 59½+ assumed (no early-withdrawal penalty on the withheld slice). The Roth tab also carries a solve-for grid: 25 conversion policies swept through the deterministic engine and ranked against your chosen objective (after-tax estate, lifetime tax+IRMAA, or widow-year tax) — reported as the model's best cell, never a directive.

The three sliders, in plain English

Taxable-account yield — money in a regular brokerage account pays dividends and interest that are taxed every year even if you never sell; the slider is your estimate of that payout rate (last year's 1099-DIV ÷ account balance; ≈1.5% for stock index funds, 3–5% for bonds and cash). No brokerage account? It does nothing. QCD modeler — only for charitable givers age 70½+: gifts sent directly from a Traditional IRA to charity never appear on your tax return and still count toward the RMD. If you don't give, leave it at $0. Roth conversion slider — lives on the Roth tab; this tab's Roth Conv column follows it live. Set the yield honestly, leave the other two at zero, and the tab is simply your projected tax life as-is.

Honest limits: SS taxation uses a simplified provisional-income test; realized cap gains default to $0 unless a sale is modeled; NIIT (3.8% on estimated investment income, unindexed thresholds), a simplified AMT check, and QCDs (a what-if slider: excluded from income and MAGI, counts toward the RMD, per-person indexed cap) are modeled.

IRMAA Cliff strategy

Medicare premium-surcharge cliffs vs your projected income.

The tier table, then a year-by-year view of MAGI vs the next cliff with a 2-year lookback ("Affects" column), headroom coloring (amber within $40K, red within $15K), and lifetime surcharge total. Driven by the Roth slider — it shows when a conversion is about to push you over a cliff and cost ~$1,000+/yr per person.

Exit Plan strategy

A five-phase operational countdown for the retirement transition itself.

Turns the plan into a sequence of moves with target dates derived from your timeline: 1 Confirm the money works (final Monte Carlo / guardrail check) → 2 Lock in health coverage (ACA bridge / Medicare) → 3 Decide & file Social Security (SSA accepts filings 4 months ahead) → 4 Put in your notice (HR checklist: PTO payout, final match, vesting) → 5 Turn on the portfolio paycheck (cash reserve → checking autopay, withholding/estimates). Each phase shows a live status chip wired to the same engine as the Events tab, plus the landmines to avoid.

▍Testing

Monte Carlo testing

The probability engine — thousands of randomized futures.

Success rate at multiple thresholds, outcome dispersion, and the shape of the 10th-percentile (bad-case) path. Uses the regime-switching model described in section 06 — plus two engine toggles, STOCHASTIC LONGEVITY and LTC DISTRIBUTION, whose full explanations (and why flipping them moves the success number) live in §06.

Five runs build the picture: A accumulation up to retirement, B the first decade, C the full 30 years (with a single long-term-care shock and deaths at life expectancy), C (no LTC) the same minus that shock so its cost is visible, and D — probabilistic long-term care, which draws a random number of care years for each spouse every run (often zero, occasionally many) instead of one fixed shock. Run D reads the harshest on purpose: it surfaces the late-life "what if care drags on for years" risk that a single early shock hides.

Historical Backtest testing

Replays your plan against real market history (1928–2025).

Survival rate across every historical start year, a stock/bond cross-check, and the infamous start years (1929, 1966, 1973, 2000, 2008, plus 1982 for contrast) with end balance, low point, and depletion year. A 1966 real-balance chart shows the worst-case grind. Complements the Monte Carlo: it replays real pasts including their actual sequencing.

Holds your asset mix constant; doesn't model taxes, RMDs, Roth, or LTC — it isolates pure sequence-of-returns risk.

What Breaks the Plan testing

Reverse stress test — solves for the break-points.

Four plain answers under the active prior: how much more you could spend, how large a one-time LTC/emergency shock you can absorb, how bad returns can get, and how many consecutive crash years at retirement you survive. Switch to BEAR to watch the edges tighten.

The modeled outflow includes estimated taxes (an annual average from the Taxes engine, including Roth-conversion taxes), claim-month-accurate Social Security, and the survivor transition (larger SS check only, plus a 25% spending drop, after the first projected death). Not modeled: recurring long-term care, IRMAA surcharges, and market sequence — the Monte Carlo tab covers that.

How bad is the return break-point, historically? The worst rolling decade for US stocks — 2000–2009, the dot-com bust followed by the financial crisis — ran about −3.4%/yr real. In 150+ years of data, no 20-year stretch has ever produced a negative real total return: the weakest windows (starting 1929, or 2000) still earned roughly +2%/yr, and every 30-year window on record has been positive (the worst ≈ +3.6%/yr, and that window ended in the depths of 1932). A break-point of several percent negative, sustained for the entire plan, therefore sits far outside anything US market history has produced. One honest caveat: those are stock figures — bonds did suffer negative multi-decade real stretches (roughly 1941–1981), which is exactly the blended-portfolio risk the Monte Carlo's stagflation regime exists to probe.

Survivor Scenario testing

The financial picture when one spouse dies — both cases.

Models the loss of the smaller SS check, the flip to Single filing (the "widow's penalty"), and the ~25% spending drop. Each case shows income before/after, the SS step-up-vs-loss mechanics, and years alone (from life expectancies) — which differ sharply between the two cases and drive how long the higher single-filer taxes apply. Argues for front-loading Roth conversions while both file jointly.

Stress testing

Named adverse scenarios.

Runs the plan through named shocks side by side — AI-bubble burst, stagflation, sequence-of-returns, a single LTC event, and the newer LTC Marathon — against a no-shock base, with Riskalyze-style risk metrics (volatility, Sharpe/Sortino, max drawdown).

In plain English — why two LTC scenarios?

The original "LTC event" assumes one big care bill ($150K-300K) fairly early, while your savings are still large. But real long-term care usually arrives at the very end of life and can drag on for years — exactly when the pot is smallest and one Social Security check has already stopped. The LTC Marathon models that long, late, rising cost. It can add up to a similar total as the single shock yet do far more damage, purely because of when it lands.

▍Tools & Reference

Ask AI ai

An AI assistant with full context on your plan.

Sends a structured summary of your data and results to a language model for natural-language follow-up. It's a real conversation: if the AI answers with a question of its own, type your reply in the same box and EXECUTE — the session transcript is re-sent each turn (last 12 messages), so it remembers what it asked. ⟲ NEW SESSION starts fresh. (Self-hosted key users: longer sessions re-send more context, so each turn costs slightly more.) Ships with five universal starter questions:

Will my money last as long as I do? What if I live longer than expected? Can I survive a crash right after I retire? How much can I safely spend each year? What if inflation stays high?

The assistant can be confidently wrong. Always verify before acting. Self-hosted copies (running outside claude.ai) power this tab with a personal API key via the LOCAL API KEY panel — stored only in that browser, never in the app file or backups, and wiped by Clear All Data. Full guide: §10.

Checklist tools

An estate & retirement-readiness checklist.

Grouped action items (estate documents, beneficiaries, account access, insurance, a survivor playbook) with notes and a contact per item. Survivor-critical items are flagged, progress is tracked, and the completion of the critical items feeds an Estate Readiness dimension on the Grade tab. Your checks and notes persist locally and travel in the Export Backup.

Skins tools

Display themes.

Seven color palettes built on a CSS-variable token system — the original Tactical Green console, three softer darks (Soft Dark Mode, Warm Executive, Low-Glare Dark), and three light paper themes: Field Manual (red, white & green), Reading Paper (warm sepia), and E-Ink Gray. The light themes are the easiest on the eyes in bright rooms and for long text-heavy sessions; the darks suit low light. Each tile previews its own colors; the choice persists in the browser cache and travels in the Export Backup.

Docs tools

This field manual.

The full documentation, viewable in-app and downloadable as HTML or printable to PDF from the toolbar above.

Verify trust

A live audit of this copy's statutory constants — run in your browser, every visit.

Every tax bracket, deduction, IRMAA tier, RMD divisor, QCD cap, wage base, and state-module fact the math depends on is re-checked against its primary-source value (IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32, CMS, SSA, IRS Pub. 590-B) the moment you open the tab, with a ✓ or ✗ per line and the citation beside it. Green across the board means this file, in your hands, right now carries the correct law — a tampered or corrupted copy fails loudly. Two longevity checks are statistical and re-sample live. Honest scope: constants, not every formula using them; the source distribution's Node suite, the behavioral tests, and eventually independent professional review cover that ground.

Events tools

Every dated obligation in the plan, as live alarms.

A live alarm for every dated obligation, derived from your timeline and the shared constants (eighteen for a two-person household — several are per-spouse) — the annual tax-constant refresh, the backtest-data append, Roth-conversion and RMD deadlines, Social Security filing windows (SSA accepts applications four months ahead), Medicare initial enrollment and annual Open Enrollment, ACA-bridge open enrollment, estimated quarterly taxes during conversion years, the peer-benchmark refresh behind the Ranking tab (the Fed SCF is triennial), quarterly backup nudges, the annual SSA earnings-record check, a January plan review, and an alarm if your for-life expenses stop before the plan horizon (which would otherwise make the simulator treat your final years as free). Statuses recompute from today's date on every load — yellow = getting close (prepare), green = action window open (go), red = action required or verify, dim = tracking / past — and nothing is stored, so alarms can never go stale or be dismissed and forgotten. The most urgent tier also surfaces as a colored strip above the tabs on every view; clicking it opens this tab. Each event carries plain-language instructions and points at the authoritative source (irs.gov, ssa.gov, cms.gov, medicare.gov, healthcare.gov). Deadlines are informational — verify with the agencies before acting.

It reads like a short situation report. The generated context includes:

Social Security (by claim age) and pension

Because it's generated from your data, the AI context stays current automatically and travels inside your exported backup — there's nothing to keep in sync by hand. \x3C!-- API KEY -->

10 Ask AI & Your API Key (Self-Hosted Copies) ↑ Contents

This section only matters if you run Danger Close on your own computer — the downloaded single-file HTML or a local dev server. Inside claude.ai, the platform signs the Ask AI call for you: there is no key, no billing setup, and the LOCAL API KEY panel doesn't even appear. On your own machine, the app has no way to prove to the AI service that anyone should pay for the answer — so you bring your own key.

In plain English

An API key works like a prepaid calling card for the AI. You open a small account with Anthropic (the AI company), put a few dollars on it, and get a secret code starting with sk-ant-. When you ask a question, the code tells Anthropic whose card to charge — typically a fraction of a cent per question. Guard the code the way you'd guard a card number: anyone who has it can spend your balance.

Getting a key (one-time, ~5 minutes)

  1. Create a developer account at console.anthropic.com. This is separate from a claude.ai login — a Claude Pro or Max subscription does not include API access. You'll verify a phone number during signup.
  2. Add a payment method and ~$5 of credit on the Billing page. Keys don't work until billing exists; the first $5 also raises your rate limit. Set a monthly spending limit while you're there — it's the single best protection against surprises.
  3. Create the key: Settings → API keys → Create Key. Name it something identifiable like danger-close. Copy it immediately — Anthropic shows the full key exactly once. If you lose it, you don't recover it; you revoke it and make a new one (painless — see rotation below).

Using it in the app

Open the Ask AI tab. In any self-hosted copy you'll see the 🔑 LOCAL API KEY panel just under the "exactly what's sent" disclosure. Paste the key, press SAVE KEY, and Ask AI is live. The panel then shows the key masked (sk-ant-••••••••1234) with a FORGET KEY button that removes it instantly.

What it costs & watching your usage

Billing is pay-per-token (a token is roughly ¾ of a word). A typical Danger Close question — your plan context in, a one-screen answer out — costs well under a cent; $5 of credit realistically lasts months of regular use. Check the Usage and Billing pages at console.anthropic.com occasionally: they show spend by day and by key. If usage ever looks unfamiliar, rotate the key (below) first and investigate second.

Where the key lives — and whether it survives closing the file

The key is kept in your browser's private storage for this app — the same place your plan data lives. It is never written into the HTML or JSX file itself, and it is never included in Export Backup. Practical consequences:

  • Normal use survives: Save & Apply, close the file, reopen the same file in the same browser → your plan and your key are still there. Nothing to re-enter day to day.
  • Sharing is safe by construction: sending someone the HTML file, or one of your .json backups, cannot leak your key — it isn't in either.
  • Some things reset it: a different browser, a private/incognito window, clearing the browser's site data, or the app's own Clear All Data all wipe the key (Clear All Data does so deliberately). Moving or renaming the HTML file may also start a fresh store, depending on how your browser scopes local files. In every such case the fix is 10 seconds: paste the key again (and Import Backup for the plan).

How safe is this? Honest answer: safe design, real residual risks

Built-in protectionsWhat they don't cover
Key travels only over HTTPS, only to api.anthropic.com — nowhere else, ever.Anyone who can use this browser profile can use the key. For the app to send it, it must be readable — so a family member on your login, a browser extension with page access, IT management software on an employer-owned machine, or malware that owns the computer could all reach it. No design eliminates this class of risk; the mitigations on the left shrink the blast radius to pocket change.
Never embedded in the file, never in backups, masked on screen.
FORGET KEY removes it instantly; Clear All Data wipes it too.
Revocable in seconds at console.anthropic.com — a stolen key dies the moment you kill it.
The three-part habit that makes this genuinely low-risk: use a dedicated key that does nothing but power this app, put a low monthly spending cap on it ($5–10), and press FORGET KEY whenever you leave the app on a shared or work machine. Worst realistic case then: someone burns a few dollars of AI credit before you revoke.

Rotating the key (replacing it)

Rotation is cheap insurance — do it immediately if you ever pasted the key somewhere by mistake, suspect the machine, or see unfamiliar usage, and consider doing it every few months purely out of caution. The whole cycle takes under a minute:

  1. At console.anthropic.com/settings/keys: revoke the old key (it stops working within moments), then Create Key for a fresh one.
  2. In the app: FORGET KEY, paste the new key, SAVE KEY.

Exactly what an Ask AI call transmits — the complete list

ItemSent?Detail
Destination—api.anthropic.com over HTTPS — or, if you've configured a Local Model, your-machine/v1/chat/completions and nothing touches Anthropic at all.
Your structured plan summaryYESThe generated context you can read verbatim under "EXACTLY WHAT'S SENT" on the Ask AI tab: names, ages, filing status, state, retirement year, portfolio totals and asset mix, account-type split, Social Security/pension amounts and claim ages, and headline simulation results.
Your questions and the running conversationYESAsk AI is a conversation: each turn re-sends the session so far (your questions and the AI's replies, capped at the last 12 messages) so the model can remember its own follow-up questions and your answers. ⟲ NEW SESSION forgets everything; nothing is stored after you leave.
Attachments you addedYESOnly files you explicitly attached (images/PDF/text; up to 8). On the Local Model route, images/PDFs are skipped — text only.
Account numbers, logins, SSNsNOThe app never collects them, so they cannot transmit.
Your API keyHeader onlySelf-hosted copies send it as an HTTPS header to api.anthropic.com only — never in the message body, never to a local model, never anywhere else.
Anything from any other tabNOOnly the summary above — not your full expense list, not position-level detail beyond the mix, not your checklist notes.
Anything, while Offline Mode is onNOThe toggle at the top of the Ask AI tab hard-disables the feature; the EXECUTE button is dead and the call cannot fire.

Offline Mode — the hard switch

Every tab except Ask AI already runs fully offline. The ✈ OFFLINE MODE toggle at the top of the Ask AI tab closes that last door: while it's on, Ask AI is disabled outright, nothing can transmit, and the app is completely air-gapped. The setting persists between sessions and works everywhere — including inside claude.ai. Use it if you want a guarantee stronger than "I just won't press EXECUTE."

Local Model — Ask AI without Anthropic (self-hosted copies)

Self-hosted copies can point Ask AI at an OpenAI-compatible server on your own computer, so your plan summary and questions go to your machine and never leave it:

  1. Ollama: install from ollama.com, pull a model (ollama pull llama3.1), and start the server with browser access allowed: OLLAMA_ORIGINS="*" ollama serve. Endpoint URL: http://localhost:11434/v1.
  2. LM Studio: load a model, start the local server, and enable CORS in its server settings. Endpoint URL: http://localhost:1234/v1.
  3. In the app: Ask AI → 🖥 LOCAL MODEL → paste the URL and model name → USE LOCAL MODEL. A violet ACTIVE badge confirms the route; BACK TO ANTHROPIC restores the default.
Honest trade-offs. Local models here are text-only (image/PDF attachments are skipped), slower on ordinary hardware, and — bluntly — markedly weaker at tax and retirement reasoning than the hosted model. The privacy is real; so is the quality drop. Whatever route answers you, verify against the tabs and authoritative sources before acting. If the call fails instantly, it's almost always CORS — revisit step 1/2.

Rotating or losing a key never touches your plan data — the two live in separate storage, and the plan's durable copy is always your exported .json backup.

Never put the key anywhere except the panel (or a git-ignored .env on the dev-server build). Not in the HTML file, not in a backup, not in an email, chat, screenshot, or code repository. Keys are personal: if someone else wants Ask AI, they create their own in five minutes. If a key ever does escape, revoke it first and ask questions after.

Running the developer (Vite) build instead? The .env proxy in the project README is the stronger option there — the key stays on the server side and never enters the browser at all.

\x3C!-- RELOAD -->

11 Reloading & Resetting ↑ Contents

  • Save & Apply (My Data tab) — writes your edits to the browser cache and rebuilds every tab.
  • Export Backup / Import Backup (My Data tab) — save your whole plan to a .json file, or load one back.
  • Clear All Data (My Data tab) — wipes the browser cache and returns you to the landing screen.
  • Your plan is cached in the browser between visits, so the app reopens straight to it — no reloading needed day to day.
The browser cache is the convenience copy; the exported .json is the durable one. Export a fresh backup after any significant change so you can always rebuild on a new browser or device.

Where your data actually lives — and how to prove it to yourself

A point worth being crystal-clear about, especially for the downloaded single-file copy: your data is never written into the HTML file itself. The file is a fixed program — you can open it, enter thirty years of financial detail, press Save & Apply a hundred times, and not one byte of the file changes. Everything you enter goes into your browser's private storage compartment for that file. That's why your plan reappears when you reopen the same file in the same browser — and why handing the file to someone else, or posting it anywhere, can never hand over your numbers.

Don't take this manual's word for it. Any of these takes under two minutes:

TestHowWhat you'll see
Two-browser testOpen the file in Chrome, enter some data, Save & Apply. Leave it open, then open the same file in Microsoft Edge (or Firefox).Edge shows the fresh landing screen — no trace of your data. It lives in Chrome's storage, not in the file. (Windows ships with Edge built in, so most machines do have a second browser even if you only ever use one.)
Private-window test (one browser is enough)With data saved, open the same file in an incognito / InPrivate window of the same browser.Fresh landing screen again — private windows get their own separate, throwaway storage.
File-properties testRight-click the file in File Explorer → Properties, and note its size and "Date modified." Use the app heavily, Save & Apply, then check Properties again.Identical size, identical date — nothing was ever written to the file.
Copy testCopy the HTML file to a USB stick and open it on another computer.Landing screen — the copy carries the program, never the data.
The flip side of that privacy: browser storage is convenient but perishable. Clearing the browser's site data, a browser reset or reinstall, a different browser, a different device — and the plan is simply gone, with no recovery. The exported .json backup is the only durable copy of your data. Export one after every meaningful change (My Data → Export Backup); Import Backup rebuilds everything from it in seconds.

The same storage model applies everywhere the app runs — claude.ai and the local dev server included. Your API key (§10) follows the same rule, with one deliberate difference: the key is excluded even from backups.

\x3C!-- HSA & MEDICARE CUTOFF -->

12 HSA Contributions & the Medicare Cutoff ↑ Contents

A Health Savings Account is the most tax-advantaged account there is — pre-tax going in, tax-free growth, tax-free coming out for medical costs. But the contribution side has a hard stop tied to Medicare, not to your retirement date. Miss it and the contributions become penalized excess. This section explains exactly when each of you has to stop.

The rule that matters

You cannot contribute to an HSA for any month you are enrolled in Medicare — Part A or Part B, and free Part A counts. Retiring changes nothing on its own; Medicare enrollment is the trigger. The two usually land close together, which is why this feels like a retirement rule when it isn't.

Being on Medicare only stops new contributions — the account stays fully usable. Withdrawals for qualified medical costs, including Medicare Part B / Part D / Advantage premiums (but not Medigap), remain tax-free for life.

Two ways Medicare starts — and when you must stop

SituationWhen Part A is effectiveLast HSA-eligible month
Claiming Social Security at or before 65Automatically at 65 — and it can't be declined while you're drawing SSThe month before your 65th-birthday month
Claiming SS / enrolling after 65Back-dated up to 6 months from your application (never before 65)About 6 months before you file — at the latest
Working past 65 on an employer HDHPDeferred until you actually enrollYou can keep contributing right up to enrollment

The 6-month look-back trap

If you delay Social Security and Medicare past 65 and then file, Part A is made retroactive up to six months (but never earlier than your 65th birthday). Any HSA contribution that falls inside that retroactive window turns into an excess contribution after the fact. The safe move: stop contributing at least six months before you file for Medicare or Social Security.

The year you stop is prorated

Your annual limit is prorated by the number of HSA-eligible months in that final year — eligible for 4 of 12 months means 4/12 of the limit, and the age-55+ $1,000 catch-up prorates the same way. (The IRS "last-month rule" can let you fund a full year if you're eligible on December 1, but it triggers a 13-month testing period — losing eligibility to Medicare the next year claws part of it back — so don't lean on it right at your cutoff.)

It can come even earlier than Medicare

Medicare is the latest possible cutoff, not the only one. Contributing also requires that you're covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan (HDHP). If you drop the HDHP at retirement — moving onto an ACA marketplace plan, a non-HDHP retiree plan, or a spouse's plan — HSA eligibility ends that month regardless of Medicare.

Where your actual dates live

The Events tab computes each spouse's exact cutoff from the Social Security claiming ages in My Data: it shows the last eligible month, whether that final year is full or prorated, and a countdown, and it raises an alarm as the date nears. Change a claiming age and the cutoff moves with it. Treat the rules here as the explanation and the Events tab as the live answer for your plan.

Not tax advice. Excess HSA contributions are taxed and carry a 6% annual excise tax until they're withdrawn. Confirm the exact stop date — and any late-year contribution — with your HSA custodian and CPA before acting.
\x3C!-- LIMITATIONS -->

13 Limitations & Known Issues ↑ Contents

  • Tax brackets are simplified. Federal bracket / standard-deduction logic is approximate; bracket inflation is modeled at 2%/yr. NIIT uses an estimated taxable-account yield (not actual dividends); the AMT check is simplified (standard-deduction add-back only); QCDs are a simplified what-if (a flat annual amount from the year each spouse turns 71; the one-time CRT/CGA election isn't modeled).
  • State tax is an approximation layer. The 51-jurisdiction module (see the Taxes tab entry) uses effective flat rates in place of progressive state brackets, treats several income-limited exclusions as unconditional, and skips county/city taxes — pick your state in My Data, then verify against your state's own rules.
  • Mortality is deterministic by default — deaths at exactly the entered life expectancies — with an optional STOCHASTIC LONGEVITY toggle on the Monte Carlo tab that samples death ages per run (see §06). The stochastic mode still samples the spouses independently — no joint-mortality correlation.
  • Long-term care is modeled two ways, both simplified. The default is a single $150K–$300K shock at a fixed age; an optional sustained model (the LTC DISTRIBUTION toggle on the Monte Carlo tab, the Stress "LTC Marathon", and Run D) draws a multi-year care duration ending at death and escalates it at inflation +1.5%/yr. Neither is a full actuarial care distribution, and insurance payouts and home equity are not credited against the cost — so the sustained figures are deliberately gross (worst-case) numbers.
  • Auto-replacement and part-time-work tapers are fixed example schedules and won't match every household.
  • Peer benchmarks are point-in-time approximations from public surveys and will go stale.
  • The Ask AI tab requires network access to the AI API; offline or rate-limited, it won't return results. Self-hosted copies also need a personal API key (§10).
  • US-only. No non-US tax residencies, accounts, Social Security analogues, or currencies.
  • The temporary OBBBA "senior bonus" deduction (up to $6,000/person 65+, tax years 2025–2028, income-phased) is NOT modeled. Its omission makes near-term tax projections slightly conservative (overstated) for moderate-income 65+ households — a deliberate simplification for a provision that expires mid-plan. Every other 2026 constant — brackets, deductions, IRMAA tiers, QCD cap, RMD table and ages, wage base — has been verified against IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32, CMS, and SSA and is asserted by the validation suite that ships with the project.
  • The BASE prior is meaningfully more conservative than historical US equity performance (see section 06). Success rates read lower than commercial tools at default settings — by design.

Two kinds of dated information — one updates itself, one needs a new file

Everything time-sensitive in this app falls into exactly two buckets, and knowing which is which tells you what maintenance it needs (short answer: almost none, and none of it is your data).

Your personal timelineThe baked-in constants
What it coversEvery alarm on the Events tab that's about you: Medicare enrollment windows, your HSA contribution cutoff, Social Security filing windows, Roth-conversion and RMD deadlines, quarterly backup nudges, the January plan review.The law-and-data numbers the math runs on: federal tax brackets and deductions, IRMAA tiers, the QCD cap, the Social Security wage base, the state-tax module, peer benchmarks, the backtest history.
How it stays currentBy itself, automatically, forever. Nothing is stored — every alarm is recalculated on every load from the dates in your plan plus today's date. Change a claiming age in My Data and every affected deadline moves instantly.Only with a new copy of the file. These numbers are printed into the app like figures in a book — the file cannot rewrite itself (that immutability is also why it's safe to share). Washington changes them about once a year.
What you have to doNothing. Keep your plan accurate in My Data; the alarms follow.When the ⌛ STALE DATA strip appears (the January after this build's tax year), you need the current HTML file. Ask the person who gave you yours — and be aware they may not have it either, if they got theirs from someone else. There is no download site yet (a permanent public download page is in the works); for now the file travels person to person, so the request may need to go up the chain to whoever maintains the app. Once you have the new HTML file, open it in place of the old one: your plan survives the swap — it lives in your browser, not the file. Export a backup first as cheap insurance.
In plain English

Think of the app as a calculator with this year's tax tables printed on the back. The calculator part never goes stale — your deadlines and alarms are computed fresh from your own dates every time you open it. The printed tables do go stale, once a year, when the IRS publishes new ones — and since the file can't reprint itself, the fix is a fresh copy of the file. You'll never have to guess when: the app tells you, loudly, with a strip across the top that won't go away until the tables are current. If someone gave you this HTML file, start with them for the fresh one — knowing they may have to ask their source in turn, since the file only moves person to person. If you maintain it yourself, the Events tab's tax-refresh alarm carries the update workflow.

Data vintages — what is baked into this build, and how it stays current

A single-file app cannot quietly update itself — a privacy feature with a maintenance cost. Every dated dataset in this build is listed here, and the app makes their age impossible to miss rather than pretending at an auto-updater:

DatasetVintage in this buildSourceRefresh cadence

Backtest return/CPI seriesThrough 2025Damodaran (NYU Stern) + BLSAnnual (Jan)
LTC cost/duration parameters2022-24 research vintageASPE / Urban InstituteOccasional

The three-layer freshness system: (1) the Events tab carries a live alarm for each refresh cycle (tax constants, backtest append, SCF release) with paste-in instructions and the authoritative source for each; (2) starting the January after this build's tax year ends, a ⌛ STALE DATA strip appears above the tabs on every view — amber the first year, red from the second — and cannot be dismissed, because stale tax law silently corrupts every projection; (3) the validation suite in the project folder asserts the constants against their cited sources, so a refreshed build proves itself. The update path is deliberately simple: download the current build and Import Backup — your data lives in the browser, not the file, so swapping the file loses nothing.

The Historical Backtest tab now provides the historical-replay capability ("what if I retired in 1966?") that earlier versions lacked.

\x3C!-- FAQ -->

14 Troubleshooting & FAQ ↑ Contents

The most common "is it broken?" moments, decoded. Almost all of them trace back to one of three things: no simulation has run yet, the browser cache was cleared, or the Ask AI tab can't reach the network.

SymptomLikely causeFix
Will Social Security run out? Should I plan on a cut?Reserve depletion is not bankruptcy — payroll taxes keep funding checks, just not the full scheduled amount (2026 Trustees Report: ~78% from late 2032 on the retirement fund alone, or ~83% from 2034 if Congress merges in the disability fund). Whether Congress acts — it always has before a cut landed — is unknowable, so the SS tab's Trust-Fund Depletion Scenario panel lets you model it instead of guessing: pick a preset or custom cut and every simulation, the Roth engine, the Dashboard, and the claiming grid recompute. Try your plan both ways; the gap between them is your personal exposure.
How do I model rental income, part-time work, an annuity, or other income?Two honest routes until a first-class income-streams module ships: a lifetime taxable stream folds into the pension amount (taxes handled; the pension is modeled without COLA), and a stream with a start/end window becomes a negative expense row (e.g., "Rental income", −1,500/mo, with dates). The negative row is cash-flow-exact; its limit is that income tax on that stream is not modeled — enter it after-tax if you can. The My Data expenses panel carries this same note.
A tab is blank or a chart is missingNo simulation has run for the selected retirement date yetPick a retirement date at the top — Monte Carlo and Stress auto-run on first visit.
Ask AI does nothing when clickedIt refuses to send until at least one simulation has completedOpen the Monte Carlo tab once, let it finish, then ask again.
Ask AI shows ERROR [4xx/5xx]The AI API received the request but refused it (rate limit, oversized attachment, outage)Wait a minute and retry. Trim attachments — 8-file cap; images, PDF, and text only (no HEIC, no Office files — export those to PDF/CSV).
Ask AI shows COMMS ERRORNo network path to the AI API (offline, blocked, or a changed endpoint)Check the connection. Self-hosted copy? Paste a personal API key into the LOCAL API KEY panel on the Ask AI tab (see its warning text). Everything else in the app runs fully offline — only Ask AI needs the network.
REQUEST TIMED OUT (45s)The question was very broad or the service is slowAsk a narrower question and retry.
All my data vanishedThe browser cache was cleared, or this is a new browser/deviceMy Data → Import Backup with your exported .json. Export one regularly — the cache is a convenience copy, not storage (see §03).
A red banner sits on every tabAn income figure is missing, so an example value was substitutedEnter the missing Social Security / pension numbers in My Data (see §04).
My success rate is far below other toolsThe BASE prior is deliberately conservative (see §06)Not a bug. Switch the scenario prior to BULL-LEANING for history-like assumptions and compare.
One edit changed numbers everywhereBy design — every tab derives from one model (see §02)Re-check the edit in My Data; Save & Apply rebuilds all 26 tabs from it.
My API key vanished from the Ask AI tabThe key lives in browser storage — a different browser, incognito window, cleared site data, Clear All Data, or (in some browsers) a moved/renamed file starts a fresh storePaste the key again (10 seconds) and Import Backup for the plan. By design the key is never inside a backup — see §10.
I think my API key leakedKeys are instantly revocable — a leaked key is only dangerous while it livesRevoke it at console.anthropic.com/settings/keys, create a new one, FORGET KEY in the app, paste the new one, and check the Console usage page (see §10).
The HSA cutoff date looks wrongIt derives from the Social Security claiming ages in My DataFix the claim ages — the Events tab recomputes the cutoff automatically (see §12).
Keeping a copy of this manual: use the toolbar above the Docs tab to download it as HTML or print it to PDF — useful if you want the reference open while working in another tab.
\x3C!-- GLOSSARY -->

15 Glossary ↑ Contents

Concise reference. Many terms have nuances this glosses over — verify against authoritative sources before acting.

4% Rule — Bengen's heuristic: withdrawing 4% of a starting portfolio (inflation-adjusted thereafter) historically lasted 30 years across most US periods. Often quoted, rarely the right answer for everyone.

ACA — Affordable Care Act. The "ACA bridge" covers a spouse between job-based coverage and Medicare at 65.

API Key — the secret code (starts sk-ant-) that identifies your Anthropic developer account when a self-hosted copy calls the AI service. Created at console.anthropic.com; treat it like a card number and see §10 for the full guide.

Agency MBS — Mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie; Treasury-level credit quality with extra yield for prepayment risk.

Asset Class — A category of investments with similar behavior (equities, bonds, cash, commodities). The MC classifies holdings this way.

Beneficiary Designation — The named recipient on a retirement account or policy; it overrides your will, so keep it current.

Bengen / 4% Rule origin — William Bengen's 1994 study established the 4% safe-withdrawal heuristic; later refined by the Trinity Study (Cooley, Hubbard, Walz 1998).

Beta — How much a holding moves relative to the market. 1.0 = moves with it; 1.5 = 50% more; 0.5 = 50% less.

Bond — A debt instrument paying interest and returning principal at maturity; provides stability and income.

Bond Tent — Pfau/Kitces idea of dipping equity exposure right around retirement, then rising again — the shape that defends the fragile early years against sequence risk.

Bond Vigilantes — Investors who sell long government bonds (pushing yields up) to protest fiscal policy.

CAPE (Shiller P/E) — Cyclically-adjusted price/earnings ratio; high CAPE has historically predicted lower forward real returns, part of the rationale for the conservative BASE prior.

Capital Gains — Profit on a sold asset. Long-term (held >1yr) is taxed at 0/15/20%; short-term is taxed as ordinary income.

CFA / CFP / CPA — Professional designations for investment analysts / financial planners / accountants. The author holds none of these.

COLA — Cost-of-living adjustment; the annual inflation raise applied to Social Security and some pensions.

Cost Basis — What you paid for a holding; sale proceeds above basis are capital gains. Inherited assets generally get a step-up to date-of-death value.

Crisis Scenario — Low-probability severe shock (2008-style). Default 3%/yr under BASE.

Crossover Age — The age at which delayed SS claiming's cumulative benefit overtakes earlier claiming. Living past it favors delaying.

DCA — Dollar-cost averaging: investing a fixed amount on a schedule regardless of price.

Drawdown — Percentage decline from a peak to a trough. "Max drawdown" is the worst such decline.

Duration — A bond's price sensitivity to rates. 6-yr duration ≈ −6% if rates rise 1%.

EBRI — Employee Benefit Research Institute; publishes the Retirement Readiness Index. Cited in Ranking.

Effective vs Marginal Rate — Marginal is the rate on your next dollar; effective is total tax ÷ total income. Roth-conversion decisions hinge on the marginal rate.

Equity — Stock ownership; "equities" = stock holdings collectively.

Estate Documents — Will, revocable living trust, durable power of attorney, healthcare proxy/advance directive, and beneficiary designations. Tracked on the Checklist tab.

ETF — Exchange-traded fund; a pooled fund trading like a stock. Most index funds are ETFs.

Expense Ratio — A fund's annual fee as a % of assets. 0.10% = $10/yr per $10K. Compounds over decades.

Fed SCF — Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; the authoritative US wealth-comparison source. Used in Ranking.

Fiduciary — Someone legally bound to act in your best interest. A fee-only fiduciary is paid only by you. The author is not your fiduciary.

FRA — Full Retirement Age; the age for full Social Security (67 for those born 1960+). Earlier reduces, later increases.

Glidepath — A planned allocation change over time. A reverse glidepath (Pfau/Kitces) starts retirement lower-equity, then raises equity to combat sequence risk.

Guyton-Klinger Guardrails — Dynamic spending rules: cut if the portfolio falls to a lower band (80% of plan), raise at an upper band (120%).

High Yield — Below-investment-grade corporate bonds ("junk"); higher yield for higher default risk.

HSA — Health Savings Account. Tax-deductible in, tax-free growth, tax-free for qualified medical use; after 65, non-medical use is taxed but not penalized.

Index Fund — A fund that passively tracks an index; typically far cheaper than active funds.

Investment Grade — Corporate bonds rated BBB-/Baa3 or higher; lower risk and yield than high-yield.

IRA — Individual Retirement Account; Traditional (pre-tax in, taxed out) or Roth (after-tax in, tax-free out).

IRMAA — Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount; a Medicare surcharge based on MAGI two years prior. Cliffs — crossing by $1 can cost thousands.

Kitces, Michael — Planning researcher; with Pfau, established the reverse-glidepath work.

LTC — Long-Term Care; help with daily activities, largely not covered by Medicare. A major risk — can run $80K–$150K+/yr/person.

LTC Duration Tail — The risk that care lasts many years and clusters at the very end of life, when the portfolio is smallest and one spouse's Social Security has stopped. A single early "LTC shock" misses it; the Stress LTC Marathon and Monte Carlo Run D exist to show it.

MAGI — Modified Adjusted Gross Income; used for IRMAA, Roth limits, and credits. Slightly different from AGI.

MBS — Mortgage-backed securities; bonds backed by pools of home mortgages.

MFJ — Married Filing Jointly; wider brackets and a higher standard deduction than other statuses.

Money Market — Cash-like instruments aiming for a stable $1 NAV; lowest risk and yield.

Monte Carlo — Running thousands of randomized projections to estimate the distribution of outcomes.

NAPFA — National Association of Personal Financial Advisors; a directory of fee-only fiduciaries (napfa.org).

NIIT — Net Investment Income Tax; an extra 3.8% on investment income above MAGI (unindexed) thresholds. Modeled on the Taxes tab from an estimated taxable-account yield.

Pension — A defined-benefit income stream from a former employer. The example has a small one; most private workers don't.

Percentile — The value below which a stated % of outcomes fall. The 10th-percentile outcome is worse than 90% of cases.

Pfau, Wade — Retirement-income researcher (safe withdrawal rates, reverse glidepaths, retirement-income frameworks).

Provisional Income — The figure (other income + half of SS) that determines how much of your Social Security is taxable.

QCD — Qualified Charitable Distribution; a direct Traditional-IRA→charity gift (age 70½+), excluded from income and MAGI, that can satisfy RMDs. Modeled as a what-if on the Taxes tab (also lowers MAGI on the IRMAA tab); 2026 cap $111K/person, indexed. Roth QCDs are permitted but pointless — Roth withdrawals are already tax-free.

Real Yield — Bond yield after expected inflation; TIPS yields are the common reference.

Recession Scenario — Moderate contraction (equity ≈ −15%). Default 10%/yr under BASE.

RMD — Required Minimum Distribution; forced taxable withdrawals from Traditional accounts starting at 73/75. A key motivation for Roth conversions.

Roth Conversion — Moving Traditional money to Roth, paying tax now for tax-free growth later. Common in low-income gap years.

Roth IRA / 401(k) — After-tax contributions; growth and qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

Roth Ladder — A multi-year sequence of Roth conversions in low-income gap years to shrink future RMDs and the widow's-penalty bracket jump.

Ruin Rate — The % of MC paths that hit $0 before the horizon ends.

Sequence-of-Returns Risk — The risk that poor early-retirement returns permanently impair the portfolio even if averages are fine. The first 5–10 years are highest-risk.

Sharpe Ratio — Excess return over the risk-free rate ÷ standard deviation. Higher is better.

Social Security — Federal retirement benefit, claimable 62 (reduced) to 70 (max). Depends on claiming age, work history, longevity.

SSA — Social Security Administration; ssa.gov is the authoritative benefit-estimate source.

Stagflation — Low growth + high inflation (1970s). The MC scenario uses negative real returns with 6–8% inflation. Default 7%/yr under BASE.

Standard Deduction — The flat amount subtracted from income before tax; larger for Married Filing Jointly than Single — the core of the widow's penalty.

Step-Up in Basis — At death, taxable assets reset to current market value, erasing the heir's capital-gains liability on prior appreciation.

Success Rate — % of MC paths ending above a threshold ($500K/$800K/$1.5M here). Not the same as ruin rate.

Survivor Benefit — When a spouse dies, the survivor keeps the larger of the two Social Security checks (not both) — a benefit cut the Survivor tab models.

TCJA — 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act; many individual provisions expire after 2025 unless extended.

Term Premium — Extra yield long bonds offer over short ones for duration risk.

TIPS — Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities; principal adjusts with CPI, giving a real yield.

Token (AI billing) — the unit AI usage is billed in, roughly ¾ of a word. A full Ask AI question and answer runs a few thousand tokens — well under a cent.

Trad / Traditional — Pre-tax retirement accounts; contributions reduce taxable income, withdrawals taxed, RMDs apply. Opposite of Roth.

Treasury — US government debt. T-bills <1yr, T-notes 2–10yr, T-bonds 20–30yr. Lowest credit risk.

Volatility — Variation in returns, usually standard deviation. Higher = wider range of outcomes.

Widow's Penalty — The tax hit when a surviving spouse files Single: narrower brackets and a smaller standard deduction on often-similar income.

Yield Curve — Yields across maturities. "Steepening" = long yields rising vs short; "inverted" = short above long (a recession signal).

Authoritative sources — Verify against ssa.gov (benefits), irs.gov (tax), medicare.gov (IRMAA/premiums), and find a fee-only fiduciary at napfa.org.
